text: Before you can appreciate why quantum error correction is hard, it helps to see the simplest error-correcting idea that actually works for classical bits — and exactly what it buys you.

The simplest possible error-correcting code is repetition. To protect a single bit, don't send it once — send it three times: encode 0 as 000, 1 as 111. The receiver recovers the original bit by majority vote, counting the 0s and 1s among the three received bits. If the true bit is 0 and the channel flips the middle bit, the receiver sees 010 — two 0s, one 1 — majority vote still says 0, fully corrected, with no need to know in advance which bit flipped. This only fails if two or more of the three bits flip. A 5-bit version tolerates up to 2 flips, at the cost of sending 5 bits instead of 3.

Computing the exact success probability directly: at a 1% channel flip rate, an uncoded bit succeeds 99% of the time, the 3-bit code 99.9702%, the 5-bit code 99.9990%. At a 10% flip rate, the uncoded bit is wrong 10% of the time; the 3-bit code cuts that down to 2.8%; the 5-bit code cuts it further, to 0.856%. Each extra layer of redundancy buys a real, computable improvement — though that improvement shrinks as the channel gets noisier.

The real cost is overhead. The 3-bit code uses 3 physical bits to protect 1 logical bit — a 3x overhead; the 5-bit code is 5x. And the benefit isn't unlimited: if the flip probability climbs past 50%, the 'majority' is more often wrong than right, and repetition backfires entirely. This tradeoff — more physical resources bought in exchange for a lower logical error rate — is the single idea this entire course generalizes. Chapter 6 runs this exact same kind of table for physical qubits protecting one logical qubit under the surface code, where the exchange rate is far steeper: hundreds to thousands of physical qubits per logical qubit, not 3 or 5.
Next lesson: why this simple, powerful idea is almost completely useless for protecting a qubit, unmodified — the bridge into everything the rest of this course builds.
